source.title: Generalization in fully-connected neural networks for time series forecasting
source.authors: A. Borovykh; C. Oosterlee; S. Bohté

record.file_problem: The full text is present. Some equations and tables have flattened formatting, but the reported table values can be assigned to their conditions.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how batch size relates to held-out performance in time-series forecasting, extending batch-size/generalization findings to a non-i.i.d. forecasting setting. It does not use the fixed-epoch-budget setup specified in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-performance results for batch-size and iteration-number settings in Tables 1–2 and describes batch-size effects in Figures 5–8. The Hessian measurements are not rows for V7: the study does not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or compare its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Results cited from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures batch-size effects at fixed SGD iteration counts in time-series regression, not V5's fixed epoch budgets. Changing batch size therefore changes the number of examples processed. Its Hessian traces and weight-scaled quadratic form do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. No other version is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors report correspondence between smaller input and weight Hessians and better generalization in their forecasting experiments, and propose learning rate, batch size and iteration count as controls for the fit–smoothness tradeoff. They also acknowledge underfitting, dataset-dependent performance effects, and the difficulty of generalizing across nonstationary time-series distributions.
record.recipe_differences: Fully connected networks trained with SGD for time-series forecasts; tests Hessian/generalization relations and training hyperparameters, rather than the image and language classification recipes in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch-size effects vary by dataset and iteration count; in the S&P500-related series the authors report no clear performance improvement from smaller batches, while temperature results favor smaller batches.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal update counts, financial forecasting has mixed batch-size results: batch 300 versus 100 gives MSE 2.76 versus 2.80 at 10000 updates and 2.71 versus 2.65 at 5000 updates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size effects on financial forecasting error are inconsistent under fixed SGD update budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: Temperature MSE increases from 0.44 to 0.49 to 0.50 with batches 10, 100 and 200 at 10000 updates; at 5000 updates it is 0.36, 0.36 and 0.37.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches can worsen temperature forecasting under fixed update budgets, with the effect depending on training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: Noisy-sine experiments associate smaller input and weight Hessian traces with smaller generalization gaps. Figure 9 also reports a linear association for the weight-scaled Hessian quadratic form, without a clearer relationship than the unscaled Hessian.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian-based curvature measures can correlate with generalization gaps in fully connected time-series regressors.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher learning rates tend to produce wider minima, with substantial overlap and outliers, but do not significantly improve test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider minima obtained by increasing learning rate need not improve forecasting performance when the resulting functions underfit.

fits_no_version.finding: An overparameterized network fits 100 Gaussian noise observations while input and weight sensitivity measures increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fully connected regression networks can fit random time-series noise by learning increasingly complex functions.

record.problems: The experiments concern time-series forecasting with dependent, potentially non-stationary data, not the natural-label image or language benchmarks in most versions. Several relations are reported through figures, and the authors describe overlap and outliers for learning-rate settings. Table values are averages over 20 sampled networks, but no uncertainty intervals are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Figure-only noisy-sine results are described in the text but lack individually recoverable numeric values; the reported relationships are summarized under fits_no_version rather than entered as numerical rows.

untested.parts: Joint demonstration of random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy above chance, and random-label held-out accuracy at chance under the same recipe. Fitting Gaussian regression noise alone does not establish this.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets, workload-dependent thresholds, and recipe adaptations on image or language workloads.
Controlled dropout comparisons, small-data effects, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance among similarly fitted convolutional networks and its ranking of generalization gaps relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both extracted V5 verdicts. The table values are valid study results, but their fixed-update comparisons cannot establish support or a scope limit for the fixed-epoch claim. Figure 9's weight scaling does not by itself make its curvature statistic the perturbation-tolerance measure specified in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
A width sweep beyond interpolation on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
The paper tests batch-size effects in time-series forecasting, but not image or language benchmarks, fixed epoch budgets, or the recipe adaptations listed in the version.
Dropout effects and removing dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: S&P500 index, interest rate and VIX returns; tested iteration and batch-size settings
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that smaller batches reduce a final-layer Hessian trace but do not seem to improve performance in this dataset; the reported MSE values also do not show a consistent batch-size effect (R1–R4). This is a time-series setting without the version's fixed-epoch image or language benchmark setup.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that smaller batch sizes have a regularising effect and that larger batch sizes correspond to worse test MSE, though the values vary with iteration count (R5–R10).
